The town library reopened last month after a renovation that took far longer than anyone had planned. The old reading room, with its cracked skylight and unreliable heating, has been replaced by a bright hall that seats 214 visitors. Librarians spent the closure cataloguing 38750 volumes, many of which had not been touched in decades. Among them they found a box of handwritten letters from a local doctor, describing an epidemic that the official records barely mention. The letters are now being scanned, and volunteers meet every Thursday evening to transcribe them. Nobody expected a building project to turn into a history project, but the staff say the discovery has brought more people through the doors than the new furniture ever could.

Growing tomatoes on a balcony sounds simple until the first heat wave arrives. A container that holds less than 19 litres of soil dries out within hours, and the plant responds by dropping its flowers. Experienced gardeners recommend watering early in the morning, shading the pots during the hottest part of the afternoon, and feeding lightly but often. One neighbour of mine keeps a notebook in which she has recorded every harvest for eleven summers; her best year produced 1463 fruits from six plants, a figure she mentions at every opportunity. She insists the secret is not fertiliser or variety but patience: she never picks a tomato until it comes away from the stem with the gentlest twist.

When the regional railway introduced its new timetable, commuters were promised faster journeys and fewer delays. The reality has been more complicated. Trains on the main line now run every 12 minutes at peak times, which is a genuine improvement, but the branch line to the coast lost its late evening service entirely. A survey of 5280 passengers found that satisfaction rose in the city and fell sharply in the smaller towns. The operator argues that it must put its limited fleet where demand is highest. Critics reply that demand follows service, not the other way around, and that a town without an evening train will soon be a town without evening visitors.

The bakery on the corner opens at half past five, long before the street lights go out. By then the first batch of sourdough has already been in the oven for forty minutes. The owner learned the trade from her grandfather, who kept the same starter culture alive for 57 years, feeding it flour and water every single day, including the day of his own wedding. She uses his recipes but not his methods of bookkeeping, which consisted of a pencil and the back of a flour sack. Last year the shop sold 91340 loaves, most of them to people who live within a ten minute walk. She has turned down three offers to open a second branch, saying that bread does not travel well and neither does she.

Astronomers have long suspected that small, cold objects far beyond the known planets could reveal how the solar system formed. Finding them is difficult because they reflect very little sunlight and move slowly against the background of stars. A recent survey photographed the same patch of sky on 136 nights and used software to stack the images along every plausible orbit. The method uncovered 742 previously unknown bodies, some of them on paths so elongated that a single circuit of the sun takes many thousands of years. The researchers are careful not to claim too much. The orbits hint at an unseen influence, they say, but a hint is not a discovery, and more observations are needed before anyone redraws the map.

Learning a musical instrument as an adult is a humbling experience. Children accept that they will sound terrible for a while; adults find it much harder to forgive themselves. My teacher, who has taught the cello for most of her life, says the students who progress fastest are not the most talented but the most regular. Twenty minutes every day is worth more than three hours on a Sunday. She asked me to keep a practice diary, and after 318 entries I can finally play a simple suite without stopping. The piece lasts barely four minutes. It took me roughly 6913 minutes of practice to get there, and I would not give back a single one of them.

The harbour authority has published its plan to protect the old quay from rising water. The proposal involves raising the sea wall by 85 centimetres, installing floodgates at the entrance to the inner basin, and replacing the wooden piles that have supported the fish market for more than a century. Engineers estimate the work will require 4725 tonnes of stone and take three winters to complete, since construction must stop during the fishing season. Not everyone is convinced. Some residents fear the higher wall will block the view that draws tourists in summer. Others point out, with some force, that there will be no view worth protecting if the market is under water.

A good map tells you where things are; a great map tells you what matters. The cartographers who drew the first detailed survey of this valley walked every footpath themselves, counting their paces and noting the position of each spring, mill and boundary stone. Their finished sheet, printed at a scale that allowed a farmhouse to be shown as a tiny rectangle, recorded 2609 named places. Many of those names have since vanished from everyday speech. A local historian is now comparing the old sheet with satellite images and has identified 173 features, mostly ponds and orchards, that no longer exist. She describes her work as a kind of translation, from a landscape people knew by heart into one they navigate by screen.

The night shift at a hospital has a rhythm of its own. Between midnight and four the corridors are quiet, the lights are dimmed, and the staff speak in lowered voices even when no patient is near. One nurse told me that these are the hours in which she does her most careful work, because there is time to sit with a frightened patient or to read a chart twice. Her ward has 26 beds and, on an ordinary night, three nurses. Over a career of many years she estimates that she has worked 3484 night shifts. She does not romanticise them, since the tiredness is real and it accumulates, but she says the mornings, when she walks home against the flow of commuters, still feel like a small private victory.

Every autumn the village holds a fair that began as a livestock market and has gradually become something harder to describe. There are still sheep, and a serious competition for the best ram, but there is also a stall selling hand bound notebooks, a tent where children build bridges out of dry pasta, and a brass band that plays the same eight tunes it has played since anyone can remember. Attendance last year reached 12870, about nine times the population of the village itself. The organising committee consists of 15 volunteers who start planning in February. Their chairman, a retired vet, says the only rule is that nothing may be sold that was not grown, made or mended within a day's walk.

Software projects rarely fail because of a single dramatic mistake. More often they sink slowly under the weight of small compromises: a test skipped to meet a deadline, a warning silenced rather than understood, a quick fix that nobody finds time to revisit. One team I worked with decided to measure this burden directly. They listed every known shortcut in the codebase and arrived at 467 items. Instead of scheduling a grand clean up, they agreed that each developer would remove one item every week, whatever else was happening. It took 94 weeks. Nothing about the process was exciting, and that was precisely the point. By the end, new features were arriving faster than before, simply because fewer things broke along the way.

The river that runs through the city was, for most of the last century, little more than an open drain. Factories discharged dye and solvent into it, and older residents remember that its colour changed with the fashions of the textile trade. The clean up began slowly, with a single treatment plant, and gathered pace when the last mill closed. Biologists who monitor the water now count 31 species of fish, including salmon, which returned without any human help. A rowing club has reopened after a gap of 68 years. On warm evenings people sit along the 1175 metre embankment with their feet above the water, an act that would once have been considered slightly mad.

Bread, cheese and wine depend on creatures too small to see, and for most of history nobody knew they were there. Cooks simply observed that dough left in a warm place would rise, that milk kept in a certain cave would ripen into something delicious, and that the same milk kept elsewhere would merely spoil. Modern laboratories can identify the organisms responsible, and a single spoonful of traditional starter may contain 53 distinct strains. Yet attempts to rebuild such a culture from purified ingredients usually disappoint. A researcher who has tried it 229 times told me that the community behaves like an orchestra: you can list every instrument and still have no idea how the music is made.

The mountain hut stands at the edge of a glacier that has retreated a little further each summer. Its guardian arrives in June, when the path is finally clear of snow, and stays until the first storms of October. Supplies come by helicopter twice a season, so everything else is carried up on foot, a climb of 1390 metres from the nearest road. The hut sleeps 44 people in two long dormitories. Guests are asked to remove their boots at the door, to be silent after ten, and to carry their own rubbish back down to the valley. In the visitors' book, between the route descriptions and weather reports, someone has written that the hardest part of any climb is deciding when to turn around.

Teaching a child to read is one of the few tasks in which the teacher gradually makes herself unnecessary. At first every word is a puzzle solved together, letter by letter. Then, usually without warning, the child begins to read silently, and the adult is left holding a book that nobody needs her to hold. A primary school in our district tracks how many books its pupils borrow over the year. Last year the total was 8215, and the most enthusiastic borrower, a girl of seven, accounted for 198 of them on her own. Her teacher says she has stopped recommending titles to her. The girl simply starts at one end of a shelf and works her way along.

There is a particular kind of silence in a workshop where someone is concentrating. The clockmaker I visited works at a bench by a north facing window, wearing a magnifying loupe pushed up on his forehead like a second pair of eyebrows. A mechanical watch contains well over a hundred parts, some of them thinner than a hair, and the one on his bench that morning had 147. He had been asked to repair it by the granddaughter of its first owner. The job would take him about 37 hours, most of it spent making a single replacement wheel by hand. When I asked whether that was worth it for an object that keeps worse time than a cheap phone, he looked at me with real pity.

Cities are warmer than the countryside around them, and the difference is greatest on still summer nights, when brick and asphalt release the heat they absorbed during the day. Planners have begun to treat shade as a public utility, in the same category as street lighting or drainage. One medium sized city has committed to planting 16437 trees over the next decade and has mapped every street by how much canopy it already has. The poorest districts turned out to have the least. Measurements taken on a single hot afternoon showed surface temperatures on a bare car park 22 degrees higher than under a row of mature plane trees a short walk away. The trees, of course, will take a generation to grow.

My grandmother kept her recipes in a tin box, written on whatever paper had been to hand: the backs of envelopes, pages torn from calendars, a bus ticket. Quantities were given in cups, pinches and, in one memorable case, the amount of flour that fits in the blue bowl. When the family decided to preserve them, we counted 283 separate slips. Testing each one took my cousin and me most of two winters. Some dishes were wonderful, and a few were frankly inedible, including a pudding that required boiling for 9 hours. We published the collection privately, with the failures left in, because a record of what people really cooked seemed more honest than a selection of what we wished they had.

Long distance cycling changes the way a person thinks about distance. A hill that a car climbs without the driver noticing becomes, on a loaded bicycle, the main event of the morning. A friend of mine rode from the northern coast to the southern border one spring, a journey of 2148 kilometres that she completed in 29 days. She carried a tent, a stove and far too many spare inner tubes, of which she used exactly one. What she remembers most is not the scenery but the kindness of strangers: the farmer who filled her bottles, the cafe owner who refused payment, the child who ran alongside for a hundred metres shouting encouragement in a dialect she could not understand.

A language does not die when its last fluent speaker does; it fades earlier, when children stop using it with one another in the playground. Linguists working on the islands off the west coast have recorded 615 hours of conversation with elderly residents, covering fishing, weather, kinship and insult, the four subjects on which the old vocabulary is richest. The recordings are being used to build teaching materials for the island school, where 43 pupils now have lessons in the language three times a week. Whether that will be enough is uncertain. One of the teachers observed that you cannot save a language by studying it, only by having something to say in it that you would not rather say in another.

The first frost of the year always catches somebody by surprise. Gardeners who meant to lift their dahlias find the leaves blackened overnight, and motorists discover that the scraper they bought last winter has migrated to some unknowable corner of the garage. Meteorologists define a frost day as one on which the air temperature falls below freezing, and the station on the hill above our town has kept such records for 127 years. In that time the average date of the first autumn frost has moved later by nearly three weeks. The keeper of the records, who has taken the readings herself on 10585 mornings, says she tries not to draw conclusions before breakfast, but the trend is hard to ignore.

Museums display only a small fraction of what they own. The rest sits in storerooms, in drawers and crates and climate controlled cabinets, waiting for a researcher to ask for it. The natural history collection in the capital holds 760 cabinets of insect specimens, each pinned above a tiny label giving the place and date of capture. For years these labels could be read only by someone standing in front of the drawer. A digitisation project has now photographed 5417 drawers, and volunteers around the world type out the handwriting from home. The data have already shown that several butterflies emerge earlier in the year than they did a century ago, a finding nobody was looking for when the pins went in.

Small theatres survive on stubbornness. The one in our neighbourhood occupies a former tram depot and has 99 seats, a number chosen because licensing rules become much stricter at one hundred. Its company of actors is unpaid, its sets are built from scrap timber, and its heating system is an act of faith. Nevertheless it has staged 352 productions since it opened, including several plays that later transferred to much grander stages. The director believes the cramped space is an advantage. When the front row can see an actor's hands trembling, she says, there is no room for anything false. Tickets cost about the same as a sandwich, and on most nights there is a queue for returns.

Before there were weather forecasts there were sayings, and a surprising number of them contain some truth. A red sky in the evening really does tend to precede a fine day in regions where weather arrives from the west. A ring around the moon often does signal approaching rain. A team of students recently tested 164 traditional proverbs against forty years of observations from a single station. They found that 21 performed better than chance, a handful were excellent, and the rest were no more reliable than tossing a coin. The most accurate of all was also the least poetic. It simply stated that tomorrow will probably be much like today, which turns out to be correct more often than not.

The ferry across the estuary takes eleven minutes and has been making the crossing, in one form or another, since long before the bridge upstream was built. Most passengers are regulars: schoolchildren, shift workers, a man who brings his bicycle and never speaks. The current vessel carries 180 people and six cars, and its engine was replaced last year with an electric motor that has cut the noise on deck to almost nothing. The skipper says the silence took some getting used to. In 23 years on the route he had learned to judge the tide by the sound of the old diesel straining against it, and now he has to look at the water like everyone else.

Insurance began, in a sense, in a coffee house, where merchants agreed to share the risk of ships that might not return. The principle has not changed: many people each pay a little so that the few who suffer a loss are not ruined by it. What has changed is the quantity of information available. An insurer today may hold 815 separate data points on a single household, from the age of the roof to the distance to the nearest fire station. This precision has a cost. As prices become more individual, the sharing becomes less real, and those who most need cover find it hardest to afford. A scheme designed for 1688 ships does not automatically suit a world in which every risk can be measured.

A well made chair is a quiet argument about the human body. Its seat must be high enough to rise from easily and low enough for the feet to rest flat; its back must support without pushing. The furniture maker whose workshop I visited has spent his career refining a single design. He showed me the first version, which he built as an apprentice, and the latest, number 526 in a series that he numbers in pencil underneath the seat. The differences are invisible unless he points them out: a rail moved by a few millimetres, a curve made slightly more generous. Each chair takes him 46 hours. He says he will know the design is finished when he can no longer think of anything to remove.

On the last day of the school year the caretaker walks through every classroom and switches off the lights, one by one. He has done this for so long that former pupils now bring their own children to the gate. The building is not beautiful, and its windows leak, and the boiler has opinions of its own, but it has taught 7392 children to read, to argue and to wait their turn. This summer the roof will finally be replaced, at a cost that occupied the governors for 14 meetings. The caretaker will supervise the work, as he supervises everything. When I asked what he would do when he retired, he said he supposed he would have to find another building that needed looking after.

Beekeepers talk about their colonies the way sailors talk about weather, with affection, suspicion and a great deal of superstition. A healthy hive in midsummer may hold more insects than a small town holds people, and the keeper who looks after the apiary behind our allotments manages 34 of them. She weighs each hive every week on a platform scale and writes the figure on the lid in chalk. Last season the whole apiary produced 1954 jars of honey, most of it sold from a table at her gate with an honesty box. She says the bees have taught her one useful thing above all others: that a problem noticed in the morning is usually small, and the same problem noticed in the evening usually is not.

The post office in the next valley was due to close, and for a while it seemed that nothing could be done about it. Then the residents formed a cooperative, bought the building, and reopened it with a cafe in the front room and the counter at the back. Membership cost very little, and 638 households signed up within the first month. The cafe now pays for the counter, the counter brings people to the cafe, and a noticeboard by the door has become the most reliable source of news for miles around. The woman who runs it says she sorted 2871 parcels in December alone. She adds that she knows who is unwell, who is lonely and who is expecting a grandchild, which is a service no delivery van can offer.
